_comment: The traps in the arenas: which ones the floor has unlocked, how many it
carries, and what standing in one costs. game/hazards.py holds the
arithmetic and none of the values, the way game/rooms.py and game/loot.py
do.
*** enabled: false IS THE ROLLBACK. ***
Switched off, no trap is ever placed, world.traps is empty, and the two
phases that read it return on a falsy test. The campaign is then the
campaign as measured before traps existed -- and BIT FOR BIT so, not
approximately so, because of the guarantee in the next paragraph.
THE HAZARD LAYER DRAWS NO DICE ON A MEASURED TICK. Placement rolls once,
at world construction, from world.hazard_rng and from nothing else. The
damage a trap deals is a flat number off the floor curve below: no damage
roll, and deliberately no crit or evasion roll either, so attr_rng is
untouched as well. A trap therefore cannot shift the sequence a damage roll
draws from however these numbers are tuned. That is the same property
progression.py has, and it is what makes the rollback exact.
UNLIKE data/rooms.json, EVERY NUMBER BELOW IS ON A MEASURED TICK. The
rooms file can say nothing here moves a bracket, because the reference bot
walks a room's entrance to its door and touches nothing. A trap is in the
arena, and the bot walks across the floor it lies on. So these numbers DO
move the grid, and where they leave it is spelled out below rather than
left for somebody to discover at the end of an eleven-minute sweep.
*** WHERE THE NUMBERS BELOW ACTUALLY LEAVE THE SUITE. READ THIS FIRST. ***
PASSING: all 280 class x stage cells, on every seed, at full strength.
No arena in the campaign becomes unclearable because of a trap.
Also passing: the face-tank ceiling, and every per-stage bracket.
FAILING, KNOWINGLY, BY DECISION:
test_the_floor_a_skilled_hero_finishes_the_whole_run
test_every_class_can_finish_the_campaign[priest]
These two are NOT tuning debt and tuning will not close them. Thirteen
configurations were swept; the score is non-monotone in every dial. Halving
the damage moved the run bracket DOWN, 4/6 to 2/6. Two seeds die on floor
20 -- a boss stage that carries no traps at all. The only configuration
that scores 6/6 is one where a trap deals 1 damage and does not move the
hero, which is not a trap.
A fixed-seed full-run pass/fail measures one TRAJECTORY through forty
fights, and any perturbation -- a point of damage, a shove, a sidestep --
sends it somewhere else. It then reports the moved trajectory in the same
units it reports difficulty. This project has hit that before: the fountain
flipped a run while the LOSING run arrived healthier. The answer then was
to keep the bot from touching the layer, and there is no version of that
for something lying on the arena floor.
So the failures were left standing rather than papered over with a third
xfail. The full argument, with the sweep table, is in docs/balance.md under
'Traps, and the limit of the run-level bracket'. If you want the suite
green in one line, it is 'enabled: false' above -- and because of the
no-dice guarantee that is the recorded campaign bit for bit.
But read what the per-stage pass MEANS. game/autoplay.py was taught to
step off a trap (_trap_underfoot), because a bot that walks down a burning
lane does not measure a hazard neutrally -- it measures it as unavoidable.
That change is inert when this file says enabled: false, and
test_the_policy_is_untouched_when_the_layer_is_off pins the hero's whole
path to prove it, so the recorded campaign is measured by exactly the
policy that recorded it.
It is still a poor trap player: half a second of lookahead, out by the
shortest open route, no idea whether it is stepping into a second trap or
into a brute. Deliberately -- it is a floor under the measurement, not a
ceiling. So a stage the bot clears is one a player certainly can.
What no sweep here will ever tell you: whether a tell is long enough to
read, whether a blade's track is legible at 1x, or whether being caught
feels like a mistake you made rather than a tax you paid. Those need hands
on a keyboard, and they are the numbers most likely to be wrong.
_harms_comment: 'hero' is a DELIBERATE ASYMMETRY and it is the one thing in this file that
is not a tuning number. Nothing in this game paths around anything --
enemies walk straight at you, which is the constraint tools/make_level.py
spends four paragraphs on. Faction-neutral traps would therefore make the
optimal play 'stand behind the spikes and let the pack funnel in', and a
deeper floor with more traps would be EASIER than a shallow one. The
mechanic would invert its own intent.
Set it to 'all' and traps become terrain that does not take sides, which
is the truer rule and the more fun one if the enemies could avoid them.
The day something in this game paths, this is the line to revisit.
_bosses_comment: Whether the eight act-enders carry traps. False, and not because a boss
with traps is a bad idea -- because those eight cells are the most tuned
in the game and the boss brain is positional (see docs/content.md). A trap
that shoves a boss fight around is a change to the most expensive thing
here, and it should be made on purpose rather than as a side effect of
_damage_comment: What one trap hit costs, by floor. Same shape as the chest payout and the
kill payout: base * (1 + floor_step * (floor - 1)), reusing the depth curve
rather than inventing a third idea of what deeper is worth.
5 at floor 3 and 17 at floor 40. For scale, a Rogue has 70 health and a
Knight 130, so a trap hit is 7% of a Rogue early and 24% of one late. That
is meant to be a mistake you feel and not a mistake that kills you, on the
grounds that a hazard which one-shots is a hazard nobody experiments with.
Conservative on purpose, and still unproven. The reference bot steps off a
trap rather than eating it, so the per-stage sweep says these numbers do
not break an arena -- it does not say they are the right numbers. Nothing
here has been felt by a person yet. Expect to tune UP once one has.
_count_comment: How many traps an arena carries: round(base + floor_step * (floor - 1)),
capped. 1 from the first unlocked floor, 2 by floor 10, 3 by floor 20, and
Capped rather than left to climb, because the placement pass draws distinct
positions from the arena's open floor and a late stage is not much bigger
than an early one. Uncapped, a floor-40 arena becomes a grid of hazards and
the thing the player is reading stops being the fight.
_rearm_comment: Ticks before one trap can hit the same body twice. 45 is three quarters of
Without it, standing in a flame lane costs sixty hits a second and every
trap is instant death regardless of the damage number. With it, a trap is
a cost per mistake rather than a rate, which is the unit the damage curve
above is expressed in and the only one worth tuning.
_spike_comment: A floor tile that blinks. Dormant 110 ticks, spikes out 40, and the cycle
is a pure function of the tick so it needs nothing saved.
Floor 3 because act I is where a mechanic gets taught and stage 3 is the
one arena whose numbers are on record -- if a spike breaks something, it
breaks it where there is a reference to compare against.
The question it asks: are you standing still? It is the cheapest of the
three to avoid and the easiest to stop noticing.
_flame_comment: Mounted on a SIDE wall -- east or west, never the top or bottom -- firing a
lane inward across the arena. reach is in tiles and the lane is clipped at
the first solid tile it meets, so a jet never burns through a pillar.
Longer cycle than the spike and a longer active window, because a lane is a
thing you cross rather than a thing you stand on: the window has to be wide
enough to still be burning when you arrive at it, or it is not a decision.
Floor 9 puts it late in act II, one act after the spike. The question it
asks: when do you cross? The spike moves your feet, this one moves your
_blade_comment: A pendulum blade on a fixed track, span tiles long, sweeping there and back
in period ticks. No active window: it is dangerous on every tick, and what
That is the whole reason it is the third one. A spike and a jet both blink,
so both are answered by waiting -- and a hazard answered by waiting is a
hazard that punishes a player for being aggressive, which is the opposite
of what this game wants. The blade cannot be waited out. The safe tile
travels, so you reposition continuously and the fight keeps moving.
It is the only trap tested against the segment it swept this tick rather
than the point it occupies (core/collision.segment_distance), because at
span 9 over 300 ticks it crosses most of its own width in a tick at the
middle of the swing and a point test would let it pass through a body.
Floor 16 is the opening of act IV, the act that puts everything together,
and it is the last new idea before the class forks at 20.
